clue.text: Guardian leaders in series ridiculing former union

parts.note: the setter writes for the Guardian, so the paper can speak of itself as US, 'we' in object form

indicators.note: the leaders of a phrase are the first letters of its words, here of the two words that follow

explanation.surface: The newspaper's editorials have been mocking the old Soviet state in a series of articles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guardian leaders' looks like the paper's editorials; instead the paper stands for US, and 'leaders in' takes the initials of 'series ridiculing'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Soviet Union was a federation of republics that dissolved in 1991, hence a former union.

clue.text: See 16 and 17
Element of matchmaking in dreadfully posh shop outside Rugby

indicators.note: the jumbled shop words go outside, wrapping round, the abbreviation for Rugby
something done dreadfully is botched, so the letters of the two words beside it come out jumbled

parts.note: RU stands for Rugby Union

explanation.surface: A horribly snobbish boutique sits beyond the town of Rugby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dreadfully' scrambles POSHSHOP into PHOSPHOS, and 'outside' puts that round RU to give PHOSPHO-RU-S.
explanation.definitionFit: Match heads are tipped with a phosphorus compound, so this element is a key ingredient in making matches.

clue.text: Put one's foot down to squash landlord's stipulation? It's lifted

definitions.text: Put one's foot down to squash

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifting the phrase turns it so it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: a tenancy rule like 'no pets' is a typical condition a landlord lays down

explanation.surface: A tenant puts a foot down against the landlord's rule on animals, which is then dropped.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's 'squash' sounds like quashing the rule, but it belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To tread on something deliberately is to crush it underfoot, a literal description of the phrasal verb.

clue.text: New ringtone's a gas!

indicators.note: making something new here means rearranging the letters of the word that follows

parts.note: the word ringtone supplies its eight letters; the 's is the verb 'is'

explanation.surface: A fresh phone ringtone is great fun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a gas' reads as slang for 'great fun', but it is literally a gaseous element.
explanation.definitionFit: This element makes up most of the air and is a colourless gas at room temperature.

clue.text: Hand in piano tune

parts.note: P is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly
an air is a melody or tune

explanation.surface: A pianist's hand moves within a tune on the keys.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hand' suggests the pianist's fingers; it is a hand of cards in poker.
explanation.definitionFit: In poker a hand holding two cards of the same rank is called by this word.

clue.text: Soldier half-buried in road above club's football field

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece sitting above another comes before it
only half of the soldier, his second letter, is sunk into the road abbreviation, while the first letter stays outside

parts.note: GI is an American private soldier
an iron is a type of golf club; the 's is 'is'

explanation.surface: A soldier is half-buried in a road beside a golf club.
explanation.walkthrough: The soldier is split: only his second letter is sunk into the road, while his first stays out in front. 'club' looks like a social club but is a golf club.
explanation.definitionFit: American football is played on a pitch marked with parallel lines, which gives it this nickname.

clue.text: What you have here is no party game

indicators.note: the game is taken with no party in it, so those letters are removed

parts.note: Cluedo is a board game of murder detection
a do is a party or social function

explanation.surface: A party game is not available here.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove DO (party) from CLUEDO, a British board game in which players deduce the murderer.
explanation.definitionFit: The reader is looking at a crossword hint right now, so 'what you have here' describes it self-referentially.

clue.text: Fudge pie's the target? Fantastic food supplier …

indicators.note: to fudge something is to fake or mess it about, so the letters that follow get rearranged

parts.note: the word gives all four of its letters, the S included
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fudge pie is the aim; what a wonderful source of food.
explanation.walkthrough: The supplier is the imaginary pasta-bearing plant from a famous BBC April Fool hoax of 1957. 'Fudge' looks like a pudding; it signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: A fanciful plant said to grow strands of pasta is indeed a made-up, fantastic source of food.

clue.text: … had 1/4 of dollar pie sent round!

indicators.note: letters sent round are spun about and come out in a different order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone got a quarter of a dollar for a pie that was passed around.
explanation.walkthrough: '1/4' looks like a quarter; in British date order it is the first of April, and 'had' means tricked.
explanation.definitionFit: Being taken in on the first of April means falling victim to the traditional pranks of that date.

clue.text: First down oddly bags last of the tricks

indicators.note: to bag something is to capture it, so the jumbled letters hold the final letter
the letters of the entry are arranged oddly, in a strange new order

parts.note: the first down clue in this grid is 1-down, the former Soviet state

indicators.note: takes only the final letter of the following word

explanation.surface: In American football, the first down strangely captures the final trick play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First down' is a gridiron term, but here it points to 1-down; 'oddly' shuffles USSR to RUSS, and 'bags' puts E inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A ruse is a deceptive trick or stratagem, so the plural matches.

clue.text: It's normal to say filthy stuff about bird in 6 27, we hear

parts.note: par is the normal or standard level, as in 'up to par'

indicators.note: the two pieces that follow are turned round together

parts.note: EG, for example, is what 'say' means in 'a fruit, say'
dirt is filth

explanation.surface: Is it usual to talk dirty about a bird we've heard of in a song?
explanation.walkthrough: '6 27' is PAIR TREE, which sounds like 'pear tree', the home of the bird in 'The Twelve Days of Christmas'. 'about' reverses EGDIRT to TRIDGE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Christmas carol's first gift is a game bird in a pear tree, which this clue points to by sound.

clue.text: King Henry appears in stage directions

indicators.note: Henry shows up in the middle of the pieces either side of it

parts.note: a step is a stage in a process
E and N are compass directions, east and north
H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance

explanation.surface: A King Henry appears in the stage directions of a history play.
explanation.walkthrough: King Henry suggests Shakespeare; the king is actually Stephen, who reigned 1135-54, and Henry is just H.
explanation.definitionFit: Stephen was an English monarch of the twelfth century, so a king.

clue.text: London team's winger replaced by northern reject

indicators.note: one letter of the team is swapped out for another letter named in the clue

parts.note: Spurs is the nickname of Tottenham Hotspur, a north London football club
the winger is the end letter of the team's name, playing out on the wing

explanation.surface: A London football club's winger is dropped for a player from the north.
explanation.walkthrough: Spurs is Tottenham Hotspur, a London football club; its last letter, the S on the wing, becomes N.
explanation.definitionFit: To spurn something is to reject it with contempt.

clue.text: Queen in gin palace, masquerading as 19 across 19 down's leader

indicators.note: the queen's letters sit inside the jumbled others
letters in disguise appear in a new order

parts.note: ER, for Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen

explanation.surface: The Queen turns up in disguise at a gin palace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'masquerading' scrambles GINPALACE and ER goes inside. The leader of San Serriffe, the Guardian's fictional 1977 April Fool island state, is named after a type size.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Guardian's spoof island republic the ruler was General Pica, a military dictator, so its leader.

clue.text: Distractedly scan Iris, Sun model? Mirror fan, probably

indicators.note: a distracted reading jumbles the letters of the next two words

parts.note: the Model T was Ford's famous car, so model gives T

explanation.surface: A girl called Iris absent-mindedly scans a tabloid's model shots.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun and the Mirror are British tabloid papers, which makes the surface about newspapers; here the mirror is a looking-glass.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone obsessed with themselves is likely to be fond of a looking-glass, hence the 'probably'.

clue.text: Part of 19 across 19 down lacking capital, reportedly

indicators.note: the answer is spoken like a phrase the clue describes

parts.note: small letters, not capitals

explanation.surface: A region of the island republic is short of funds, they say.
explanation.walkthrough: In the spoof state the two islands are named for printing terms: small letters are lower case, spelt here with the French 'caisse'.
explanation.definitionFit: San Serriffe consisted of two islands, the southern one bearing this name in the Guardian's spoof.

clue.text: State capital for part of 19 across 19 down

indicators.note: to state a word is to say it, so the answer sounds like the next words

parts.note: a capital letter is in ... case

explanation.surface: A state capital is named as a region of the republic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State capital' reads as a seat of government; it means 'say capital letters', upper case, spelt with the French 'caisse'.
explanation.definitionFit: San Serriffe consisted of two islands, the northern one bearing this name in the Guardian's spoof.

clue.text: Where 9 was "harvested" by soldiers in republic

indicators.note: the soldiers are placed inside the republic

parts.note: Panama is a Central American republic
OR, other ranks, means soldiers who are not officers

explanation.surface: Soldiers in a republic harvested something somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The BBC current-affairs programme of this name broadcast the 1957 spaghetti harvest hoax.
explanation.definitionFit: The BBC's long-running documentary show aired the famous spoof film of Swiss farmers picking pasta.

clue.text: King featuring in naff series about republic

indicators.note: the king appears inside the jumbled letters
the letters of the two words are moved about

parts.note: R, for Rex, means king

explanation.surface: A king stars in a rubbish TV series about a republic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'naff' is British slang for tacky. The answer is the Guardian's fictional island republic from its April Fool supplement of 1977.
explanation.definitionFit: The spoof nation was presented as an island republic in the Indian Ocean.

clue.text: See 19 across
Frenchman initially wanted to start again

parts.note: Rene is a typical French man's name

indicators.note: takes the first letter of the word after it

explanation.surface: A Frenchman at first wanted to begin afresh.
explanation.definitionFit: To renew is to resume or begin something once more.

clue.text: New nurse keeps working to get one off drugs

indicators.note: the jumbled word holds another piece inside it
a new version of the word is an anagram of it

parts.note: a machine that is on is working

explanation.surface: A newly qualified nurse keeps working to get someone off drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' does double duty in the surface as 'newly qualified', but it is purely the anagram signal for the nurse.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who no longer takes something, such as drugs, is a non-user of it.

clue.text: More concise instructions to retreating troops

parts.note: a brief is a set of instructions

indicators.note: retreating means going backwards, so the troops are read in reverse

parts.note: RE, the Royal Engineers, are British army troops

explanation.surface: Shorter orders are given to troops in retreat.
explanation.definitionFit: Briefer is the comparative of brief, meaning shorter or more succinct.

clue.text: Blood count is taken regularly in 19 across 19 down. Capital!

indicators.note: every other letter of the following words is taken, starting with the first

explanation.surface: A blood count is taken at regular intervals; splendid!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital!' looks like an exclamation meaning 'excellent'; it is the capital city of the spoof island, named after a typeface.
explanation.definitionFit: In the spoof, the chief city of the island republic shared its name with a classic serif typeface.

clue.text: See 10
Wasted away as a left back at Hyde, say

indicators.note: the word for left is sent back, so it is read in reverse

parts.note: port is the left side of a ship

indicators.note: the town name is said, giving a word that sounds alike

parts.note: Hyde is a town near Manchester, which sounds like hied, meaning hurried

explanation.surface: A left-back at a Hyde football club played wastefully.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left back' looks like a football position; it is PORT reversed. Hyde, a town near Manchester, sounds like HIED.
explanation.definitionFit: Atrophied describes body tissue that has withered or shrunk through disuse.

clue.text: A large number on doctor's round?

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece on top of another comes first

parts.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand
MO, medical officer, is a doctor

explanation.surface: Many patients are on a doctor's rounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' looks like a doctor's visits; here it is a round of ammunition.
explanation.definitionFit: A round is a single cartridge or shell, and the answer is slang for ammunition.

clue.text: See 14
Call model instead of hospital porter?

indicators.note: one letter takes the place of another in the word given by Call

parts.note: to shout is to call out
the Model T was Ford's famous car, so model gives T

explanation.surface: Should one call a model in place of a hospital porter?
explanation.walkthrough: 'hospital porter' looks like a hospital worker; porter is a dark beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Stout and porter are both dark beers brewed with roasted malt.

clue.text: See 9
Ape caught by Frenchwoman

indicators.note: caught sits next to the Frenchwoman, following her

parts.note: Mimi is a French woman's name, as in La Boheme
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: An ape has been captured by a Frenchwoman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ape' looks like a noun for the animal; it is the verb, to copy.
explanation.definitionFit: To ape someone is to copy their manner, which is what a mimic does.

clue.text: French department with some berets in? I flew round

indicators.note: the run is turned round, read from right to left
some of the letters of the phrase are taken, a run within it

explanation.surface: Wearing berets, I flew around a part of France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' reverses the run ERETSINIF found in 'berets in? I flew'. Finistere is in Brittany.
explanation.definitionFit: Finistere is an administrative department at the western tip of Brittany in France.
